headline: The spray FDA
warned about.
dek: No topical finasteride is FDA approved. In 2025 FDA warned about the compounded ones.
photoAlt: Illustration for the Hair loss lane.

glance.label: Compounded sprays
glance.line: Finasteride and minoxidil mixed with other drugs: not FDA approved.

src.label: FDA alert on compounded topical finasteride, Apr 2025

glance.label: Side effects
glance.line: Lower libido and erection problems on the label; suicidal thoughts added in the EU in 2025.

pull.quote: There are no FDA-approved topical products with finasteride alone or in combination with other ingredients.

body: In April 2025, FDA sent a warning to health care providers, compounders and consumers about a hair-loss product that had become easy to order online: [[/finasteride|finasteride]] made up by a pharmacy to go on the scalp. The agency said it was aware of “some compounders and telemedicine platforms that market topical formulations of finasteride”[^fdaalert], alone or mixed with [[/minoxidil|minoxidil]]. Its conclusion was blunt: “There are no FDA-approved topical products with finasteride alone or in combination with other ingredients.”[^fdaalert]

The warning grew out of reports from patients. FDA said “There were 32 cases reported to the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System between 2019 and 2024.”[^fdaalert] The problems described matched those known from finasteride tablets, among them erectile dysfunction, anxiety, suicidal thoughts, brain fog, depression and lower sex drive. FDA added that “Most of the reports FDA has received state the adverse events continued to persist after product discontinuation.”[^fdaalert]

There was a second worry. Finasteride can cause abnormalities in a male fetus, so the approved tablets are coated, and women are told not to handle crushed or broken ones. FDA noted that “compounded topical finasteride products do not have a coating,”[^fdaalert] and it pointed to a greater risk of exposing others, especially women, through transfer of the applied product.[^fdaalert]

What FDA has approved is narrower. Finasteride tablets were approved as Proscar, for an enlarged prostate, on June 19, 1992, and as Propecia, for hair loss, on December 19, 1997.[^fdaalert] The Propecia label limits it to male pattern hair loss “in MEN ONLY”[^propecia] and says it “is not indicated for use in women.”[^propecia] The approval rested on three studies in 1,879 men with mild to moderate hair loss.[^propecia] Minoxidil solution for the scalp was approved as Rogaine in August 1988.[^rogaine]

Finasteride’s side effects are printed on its label. In the trials, 36 of 945 men on Propecia, or 3.8%, reported one or more sexual side effects, such as lower libido or erection problems, against 20 of 934 men, or 2.1%, on placebo.[^propecia] Since approval, the label adds, there have been reports of “sexual dysfunction that continued after discontinuation of treatment”[^propecia], along with depression and suicidal thoughts and behavior.[^propecia]

Regulators in Europe went further. In 2025, after an EU-wide review, EMA’s drug-safety committee confirmed suicidal thoughts as a side effect of finasteride 1 mg and 5 mg tablets, and said “The frequency of the side effect is unknown”.[^ema] Most cases were reported in men taking the 1 mg tablets for hair loss.[^ema] In May 2026 the UK’s MHRA advised that “patients prescribed finasteride 1 mg should stop taking the medicine if they develop suicidal thoughts or depression and contact their healthcare professional as soon as possible”.[^mhra]

Many men now take minoxidil as a pill, which is off-label. Minoxidil tablets are approved for severe high blood pressure, and their label warns that the drug “can cause pericardial effusion, occasionally progressing to tamponade,”[^minoxtab] a build-up of fluid around the heart. It also says that “Use of minoxidil tablets, in any formulation, to promote hair growth is not an approved indication.”[^minoxtab] One randomized trial in Brazil enrolled 90 men and compared 5 mg a day by mouth with a 5% solution on the scalp twice a day for 24 weeks.[^penha] The authors wrote that the pill “did not demonstrate superiority over topical minoxidil”.[^penha]

[[/dutasteride|Dutasteride]], a close relative of finasteride, is approved in the US as Avodart only for an enlarged prostate.[^avodart] Japan approved it as Zagallo for male pattern hair loss on September 28, 2015.[^pmda] In a 24-week trial of 917 men aged 20 to 50, men on dutasteride 0.5 mg had higher hair counts than men on finasteride 1 mg or placebo.[^harcha] In the US, taking it for hair loss is off-label.

Newer drugs aim to block male hormones only in the scalp. [[/clascoterone|Clascoterone]] is FDA approved as Winlevi, a cream “indicated for the topical treatment of acne vulgaris in patients 12 years of age and older.”[^winlevi] It is not approved for hair loss. A solution of it was tested for male pattern hair loss in two six-month Phase 3 trials, SCALP1 with 703 people and SCALP2 with 762.[^scalp1][^scalp2] [[/pyrilutamide|Pyrilutamide]], also called KX-826 has been in a Phase 3 trial of 740 men in China.[^kx826]

[[/ru58841|RU58841]] is older and much less studied. Researchers at Roussel Uclaf in France described it in 1994 as a candidate for acne, hair loss and excess hair growth.[^ru1994] The search found no published trial of it in people with hair loss as of November 1, 2026.[^rupubmed][^ructg] The only human study, published in 2026, applied a hair product containing it once to the scalp of six healthy men to see how the body breaks it down.[^okutan]

A different condition has seen the most new approvals. Alopecia areata is an immune disease in which hair falls out in patches. FDA has approved three JAK inhibitor pills for severe alopecia areata: [[/baricitinib|baricitinib]] (Olumiant), [[/ritlecitinib|ritlecitinib]] (Litfulo) and [[/deuruxolitinib|deuruxolitinib]] (Leqselvi).[^olumiant][^litfulo][^leqselvi] Their labels open with a boxed warning about “SERIOUS INFECTIONS, MORTALITY, MALIGNANCY, MAJOR ADVERSE CARDIOVASCULAR EVENTS (MACE), and THROMBOSIS”.[^litfulo]

Supplements are the least tested of all. FDA says that “FDA does not have the authority to approve dietary supplements before they are marketed.”[^dsq] For [[/saw-palmetto|saw palmetto]], NIH’s complementary health center says a few small studies have tested it for male pattern hair loss and that “The evidence is too limited to allow conclusions to be reached.”[^nccih] For [[/pumpkin-seed-oil|pumpkin seed oil]], one randomized trial gave 76 men 400 mg a day or a placebo for 24 weeks and reported more hair in the oil group.[^cho]

What is still not known is how often finasteride’s lasting side effects happen, since the reports are voluntary and EMA says the frequency cannot be estimated.[^ema] Nor is it known how compounded scalp mixtures behave. As FDA put it, “Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means FDA has not evaluated their safety, effectiveness or quality prior to marketing.”[^fdaalert]
